Meaning 1: To walk a long distance, especially in nature

This is the most common meaning. When you hike, you walk a long distance — usually through mountains, forests, hills, or countryside. It is not just any walk. It carries the sense of physical effort, distance, and being in an outdoor, natural setting.

Examples:

  • "We hiked through the forest for six hours."
  • "She hiked along the river trail every weekend."
  • "They hiked ten miles before setting up camp."

What separates hiking from ordinary walking:

  • The terrain is usually uneven, steep, or rough — not a flat city pavement.
  • It takes much longer — usually hours.
  • It involves noticeable physical effort.
  • It happens in nature, and often for recreation or adventure.

You can also say "go hiking" (this is equally common):

  • "Let's go hiking this Sunday."
  • "Have you ever gone hiking in the mountains?"

Both mean the same thing — the only difference is phrasing.
Meaning 2: To raise or increase something sharply

In this sense, "hike" means to increase a price, rate, tax, salary, or fee — usually by a large amount, and often suddenly or unexpectedly. This meaning is very common in news, business, and economic conversation.

Examples:

  • "The government hiked fuel prices by 20%."
  • "The central bank hiked interest rates to slow down inflation."
  • "The landlord hiked the rent without warning."
  • "Airlines hiked ticket prices during the holiday season."

Important nuance — tone: Saying someone "hiked" a price sounds more alarming and dramatic than saying they "raised" or "increased" it. The word "hike" quietly suggests that the increase is steep, unwelcome, or abrupt. Journalists and writers use it precisely for this reason — it adds a sense of urgency or criticism.

So: "The company raised its prices" feels neutral. "The company hiked its prices" sounds sharper — almost like a complaint.

What can be "hiked" in this sense: Almost always something measurable — prices, fares, fees, taxes, interest rates, wages, costs. You would not use "hike" for vague or abstract things.
Meaning 3: To pull something upward sharply

This meaning is more physical and everyday. When you "hike" something, you grab it and pull it up firmly and quickly — usually a piece of clothing that has slipped down or needs to be raised.

This meaning almost always appears as the phrasal verb "hike up", not "hike" alone.

Examples:

  • "She hiked up her skirt to cross the muddy stream."
  • "He hiked up his trousers before kneeling on the floor."
  • "The child hiked up his socks."

The image is of a quick, firm yank upward — not a slow, gentle lift.
The Phrasal Verb "Hike Up" — Used for Both Meaning 2 and Meaning 3

You will notice that "hike up" works for both:

  • "They hiked up the prices." → raised the prices (Meaning 2)
  • "She hiked up her sleeve." → pulled her sleeve up (Meaning 3)

The context makes it clear which meaning is intended. If it is followed by clothing, it means to pull up. If it is followed by a price, cost, rate, or fee, it means to raise.
Register and Tone — When Is Each Meaning Used?

Nature/walking sense: Used in both casual and formal speech. Universally common.

Price/rate sense: Very common in journalism, economics, and business conversation. Carries a slightly negative, dramatic tone — implying the increase was large or unwelcome. Not used for small, expected increases.

Pull-up sense: Casual and informal, mostly in everyday spoken or written language.
The Three Meanings at a Glance

1. Walk long distances in nature → "They hiked the mountain trail."
  2. Raise prices/rates sharply → "The bank hiked interest rates."
  3. Pull clothing upward → "He hiked up his trousers."
